claims.claim: Robert K. Merton's 'Social Structure and Anomie' was published in the American Sociological Review, volume 3, number 5, October 1938, pages 672-682, while he was at Harvard University.

Merton distinguished two elements of social and cultural structure - culturally defined goals, which form a frame of aspirational reference, and the institutional norms regulating the acceptable modes of reaching them - and argued that deviance becomes more common when emphasis on a culturally induced success goal is divorced from a coordinated institutional emphasis.

Merton set out five modes of adjustment or adaptation in a table on page 676 - I. Conformity (+ culture goals, + institutionalized means), II. Innovation (+, -), III. Ritualism (-, +), IV. Retreatism (-, -), V. Rebellion (plus-or-minus on both) - where (+) signifies acceptance, (-) signifies elimination, and (plus-or-minus) signifies rejection and substitution of new goals and standards.
Merton wrote that in every society Adaptation I, conformity to both culture goals and means, is the most common and widely diffused, and that Adaptation IV, retreatism, is the least common.

Merton warned immediately after presenting the table that persons may shift from one alternative to another as they engage in different social activities, and that the categories refer to role adjustments in specific situations rather than to personality in toto.

Merton identified innovation - retaining the success aspiration while relinquishing the institutional means - as his major concern, and located its structural source in the limitation of opportunity to unskilled labour combined with the cultural stigmatisation of manual labour.

Merton closed the 1938 article by listing what it had not done, including that it had not tested the full explanatory power of the scheme against a large number of group variations in the frequency of deviate and conformist behaviour.

Emile Durkheim used anomie for a state of deregulation in which traditional rules lose their authority; in Suicide (1897) he tied anomic suicide to the 'mal d'infini', the condition arising when society stops setting limits on legitimate aspirations for wealth, goods, and pleasure, so that desires go unregulated and expectations no longer correspond with reality. His doctoral thesis On the Division of Social Labor appeared in 1893 and Suicide in 1897.

Merton adapted Durkheimian anomie: culturally promoted goals such as the American Dream are unevenly reachable because social structure restricts some people's opportunities, and the disjunction between a society's goals and the appropriate means of achieving them produces pressure or strain.

The classic strain tradition is conventionally identified with Merton (1938), Albert K. Cohen's Delinquent Boys (1955), and Cloward and Ohlin's Delinquency and Opportunity (1960); Agnew names these three as the models on which most empirical studies of strain theory continued to rely as of 1992.

Cohen (1955) argued that strain can come from a lack of status: lower-class youths who cannot meet middle-class standards experience status frustration and seek status and self-worth in an alternative value system shared with peers.

Cloward's 1959 American Sociological Review article 'Illegitimate Means, Anomie, and Deviant Behavior' (volume 24, number 2, April 1959, pages 164-176) introduced the argument, developed with Ohlin in Delinquency and Opportunity (1960), that illegitimate opportunities are also unequally distributed, and Cloward and Ohlin distinguished criminal, conflict, and retreatist gang subcultures.

Agnew's 'Foundation for a General Strain Theory of Crime and Delinquency' appeared in Criminology, volume 30, number 1, February 1992, pages 47-87, and described three major types of strain: the actual or anticipated failure to achieve positively valued goals, the actual or anticipated removal of positively valued stimuli, and the actual or anticipated presentation of negatively valued stimuli.

Agnew opened the 1992 article by observing that after dominating deviance research in the 1960s, strain theory came under heavy attack in the 1970s, with prominent researchers - he names Hirschi (1969) and Kornhauser (1978) - suggesting the theory be abandoned, and that although it survived, its influence was much diminished.

Agnew built general strain theory on research outside criminology: stress research in medical sociology and psychology, equity and justice research in social psychology, and aggression research including recent versions of frustration-aggression.

In general strain theory the pathway from strain to crime runs through emotion: strains, especially subjective strains, produce negative emotions such as anger and frustration, and those emotions create pressure for corrective action, of which crime is one possible form.

Agnew (2001) specified that strains are most likely to result in crime when they are seen as unjust, are seen as high in magnitude, are associated with low social control, and create some pressure or incentive to engage in criminal coping.

Agnew states that criminal coping is more likely among people with poor coping skills and resources, few conventional social supports, low social control or little to lose, a disposition to criminal coping including criminal associates, beliefs favourable to crime, and traits such as low constraint and negative emotionality, and in situations where the perceived costs of crime are low and the benefits high.

Agnew and White (1992), using data from 1,380 New Jersey adolescents, reported qualified support for general strain theory: strain measures of the three specified types had a relatively substantial effect on delinquency and drug use, and the effect was conditioned by association with delinquent peers and by self-efficacy, as the theory predicted.

Burton and Cullen's 1992 review reported that empirical tests of strain theory had yielded mixed results, with the level of support varying by the measure used to operationalise strain, and that methodological limitations of existing studies complicated any assessment of the theory's utility.

Classic strain theory was most often tested indirectly, through the disjunction between aspirations and expectations; Agnew, Cullen, Burton, Evans and Dunaway (1996) argued that the variable the theory actually names - dissatisfaction with one's monetary status - had been ignored in virtually all tests, and when they measured it directly in a sample of Cincinnati adults it predicted income-generating crime and drug use, giving what they called qualified support unlike much previous research.

Most studies find that individual economic status is unrelated or only weakly related to individual offending, a result that has been used to challenge the validity of classic strain theory; Agnew argues the relationship is modest over much of the range of economic status but substantial for the very poor.

Agnew (2001) conceded that researchers testing general strain theory have little guidance when selecting among the many hundreds of types of strain and have trouble explaining why only some of them are related to crime, so that measures of 'strain' differ widely across studies.

Froggio's 2007 review of the evidence accumulated on general strain theory between 1992 and 2003 described the theory as a social-psychological interpretation of juvenile delinquency with a solid conceptual basis, and characterised its review as a first critical evaluation of the theory's empirical status.

Messner and Rosenfeld's institutional anomie theory, set out in Crime and the American Dream, contends that culturally and structurally produced pressures to secure monetary rewards, combined with weak controls from non-economic social institutions, promote high levels of instrumental crime.

Chamlin and Cochran (1995), testing institutional anomie theory with cross-sectional data for U.S. states, reported considerable but indirect support: the effects of poverty on property crime depended on structural indicators of the capacity of non-economic institutions to ameliorate economic deprivation. Messner and Rosenfeld applied the theory cross-nationally to homicide in Social Forces in 1997.

Mertonian strain is a structural theory - it explains differing rates of deviance across a society's groups from the arrangement of cultural goals and legitimate means - while general strain theory is largely social-psychological, explaining an individual's offending through disliked events and conditions, the emotions they generate, and personal coping resources.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Merton's five adaptations are personality types.
positions: The SOU-CCJ230 open textbook chapter labels the table 'Personality Adaptation'.

Merton, on page 676 of the 1938 article, wrote that persons may shift from one alternative to another across different social activities and that the categories refer to role adjustments in specific situations, not to personality in toto.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The primary source governs. The lesson presents the adaptations as situational role adjustments and flags the personality reading as a common mistake.

positions: Crossref records the article as Criminology 30(1):47-88.
The NCJRS bibliographic record (NCJ 136257) gives Criminology 30(1):47-87 and a length of 41 pages.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: 47-87 is used; 47 to 87 inclusive is 41 pages, matching the NCJRS length field. The Crossref end page is treated as an exclusive-endpoint artefact.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strong the empirical support for general strain theory is.
positions: Agnew and White (1992) reported a relatively substantial effect of strain on delinquency and drug use, conditioned as predicted.

Burton and Cullen (1992) found strain research mixed and highly sensitive to operationalisation; Agnew (2001) conceded that the choice among hundreds of candidate strains is under-specified; Froggio (2007) still treated the theory's empirical status as unsettled after a decade.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that general strain theory has fared better in testing than classic strain theory, reports the specific verified findings, and says plainly that effects are modest and that 'strain' is measured very differently across studies. No meta-analytic effect size is asserted, because none could be verified against a retrievable source during this research session.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing substantive about strain theory. Its In 30 Seconds, Why This Matters, College Version, vocabulary, Eli-10, worked example, mistakes and questions were topic-agnostic boilerplate that named no theorist, no date, and no finding, and none of it was carried forward.
The draft's vocabulary entry defined 'Strain Theory' as 'a foundational Criminal Justice & Criminology concept covered in this lesson', which is circular and was discarded.
The draft's Eli-10 lacked analogyLimits entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with sourced content; the only element retained is the topic title.

Verified Merton's typology against a scan of the original 1938 American Sociological Review article rather than reproducing a remembered table: the order is Conformity, Innovation, Ritualism, Retreatism, Rebellion, and the signs denote acceptance, elimination, and rejection-with-substitution rather than a simple accept/reject.
Corrected the widespread 'personality adaptation' framing against Merton's own caveat about role adjustments in specific situations.

A first automated read of the Merton PDF returned a plausible-sounding but unverifiable summary; the file turned out to be an image-only JSTOR scan whose extractable text was the cover page alone. Page images were rendered and read directly before any claim about the typology was written.
Dated and attributed every element: Durkheim 1893/1897, Merton 1938, Cohen 1955, Cloward 1959, Cloward and Ohlin 1960, Agnew 1992, Messner and Rosenfeld 1994, Agnew 2001.
Stated the empirical record honestly in both directions rather than presenting strain theory as an established explanation of crime.
Added an explicit statement that the lesson is educational material and takes no policy position.

sourceRecords.title: Social Structure and Anomie, American Sociological Review 3(5):672-682 (October 1938)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert K. Merton, American Sociological Association
sourceRecords.notes: The lesson's primary source for classic strain theory, read page by page. The canonical record is the DOI; the copy actually read was the JSTOR page-image scan of the original 1938 printing posted at http://www.csun.edu/~snk1966/Robert%20K%20Merton%20-%20Social%20Structure%20and%20Anomie%20Original%201938%20Version.pdf. That PDF carries no usable text layer, so the embedded page images were extracted and read directly. Verified from the document itself: the JSTOR cover page giving American Sociological Review Vol. 3, No. 5 (Oct., 1938), pp. 672-682; Merton's Harvard affiliation; the opening rejection of the biological-drives account of deviance and the aim of showing how some social structures exert a definite pressure toward nonconformity; the two elements of social and cultural structure (culturally defined goals as a frame of aspirational reference, and the institutional norms regulating acceptable modes of reaching them); the competitive-athletics illustration and the point that the rules of the game are known to those who evade them; the page-676 table of five modes of adjustment or adaptation with the sign conventions (+ acceptance, - elimination, plus-or-minus rejection and substitution of new goals and standards) and the ordering Conformity, Innovation, Ritualism, Retreatism, Rebellion; the immediately following caveat that persons shift between alternatives and that the categories refer to role adjustments in specific situations, not to personality in toto; the page-677 statements that Adaptation I is the most common and widely diffused in every society and Adaptation IV the least common; the page-678 characterisations of innovation, ritualism and rebellion, the declaration that the major concern is with the illegitimacy adjustment, and the argument that limitation of opportunity to unskilled labour plus the cultural stigmatisation of manual labour produces a strain toward innovational practices; and the page-682 closing list of what the paper had not done, including that it had not tested the scheme against a large number of group variations. Copyrighted; no prose reproduced beyond the adaptation names and the two table column headings, which function as proper names.

sourceRecords.title: Emile Durkheim (1858-1917), Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sourceRecords.provider: Paul Carls, University of Montreal, for the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (ISSN 2161-0002)
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed philosophy encyclopedia entry, retrieved and read on 2026-08-19 with a browser user-agent. Supports the Durkheim background only: that Durkheim's term for the breakdown of morality is anomie, a state of deregulation in which traditional rules have lost their authority; that anomic suicide involves the 'mal d'infini', arising when society stops defining what count as legitimate aspirations regarding wealth, material goods and other pleasures, so that the passions go unregulated and the individual's expectations do not correspond with reality; and the publication years of On the Division of Social Labor (1893), The Rules of Sociological Method (1895) and Suicide: A Study in Sociology (1897). Durkheim's own works were not read for this lesson, so the lesson asserts nothing about them beyond what this entry states. No wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 5.9. Strain Theories, in SOU-CCJ230 Introduction to the American Criminal Justice System
sourceRecords.provider: Brian Fedorek, in Burke, Carter, Fedorek, Morey, Rutz-Burri & Sanchez (Open Oregon Educational Resources / Pressbooks)
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record, reused with its id and URL unchanged. Read in full on 2026-08-19 as corroboration for the chain of attribution: Durkheim's anomie as normlessness following rapid social change; Merton (1938) adapting Durkheimian anomie to the American success goal and the disjunction between goals and approved means; Cohen (1955), Delinquent Boys: The Culture of the Gang (Free Press), on status frustration among lower-class youths who reject middle-class values and seek status in an alternative value system; Cloward and Ohlin (1960), Delinquency and Opportunity: A Theory of Delinquent Gangs (Free Press), on illegitimate opportunity and the criminal, conflict and retreatist gang types; and Agnew's three strains leading to negative emotions such as anger, depression and fear, with crime as a way of venting when prosocial coping is unavailable. This chapter labels Merton's table 'Personality Adaptation'; that label conflicts with Merton's own text and is not followed. No wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Illegitimate Means, Anomie, and Deviant Behavior, American Sociological Review 24(2):164-176 (April 1959)
sourceRecords.provider: Richard A. Cloward, American Sociological Association
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record verified through the Crossref API on 2026-08-19: Richard A. Cloward, American Sociological Review, volume 24, issue 2, April 1959, first page 164. Cited for the authorship, date and subject of the article in which Cloward introduced illegitimate means into the anomie tradition, the argument later developed with Lloyd Ohlin in Delinquency and Opportunity (1960). The full text is paywalled and was not read; the lesson's substantive description of differential opportunity rests on the SOU-CCJ230 chapter and the Agnew (2015) handbook chapter, and this record supports only the citation.

sourceRecords.title: Foundation for a General Strain Theory of Crime and Delinquency, Criminology 30(1):47-87 (February 1992)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert Agnew, American Society of Criminology / Wiley
sourceRecords.notes: The founding statement of general strain theory. Full text paywalled. The publisher abstract was retrieved verbatim through the Crossref API, and the Semantic Scholar Graph API returned the abstract together with the article's opening paragraphs. Supports: the three major types of strain as the actual or anticipated failure to achieve positively valued goals, the actual or anticipated removal of positively valued stimuli, and the actual or anticipated presentation of negatively valued stimuli; that the paper distinguishes strain theory from social control and differential association/social learning theory, gives guidelines for measuring strain, and discusses the factors influencing the choice of delinquent versus nondelinquent adaptations; that after dominating deviance research in the 1960s strain theory came under heavy attack in the 1970s, with prominent researchers - Hirschi (1969) and Kornhauser (1978) are the ones Agnew names - suggesting it be abandoned, and that its influence was much diminished by 1992; that most empirical studies then still relied on the models of Merton (1938), A. Cohen (1955), and Cloward and Ohlin (1960); and that Agnew drew on stress research in medical sociology and psychology, equity and justice research in social psychology, and aggression research including recent versions of frustration-aggression. Pagination cross-checked against the NCJRS record (NCJ 136257), which gives 47-87 and a length of 41 pages; Crossref's 47-88 is treated as an exclusive endpoint. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: An Empirical Test of General Strain Theory, Criminology 30(4):475-500 (November 1992)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert Agnew and Helene Raskin White, American Society of Criminology / Wiley
sourceRecords.notes: Publisher abstract retrieved verbatim through the Crossref API and confirmed through OpenAlex on 2026-08-19; full text paywalled. Supports the first direct test of general strain theory: data from a sample of 1,380 New Jersey adolescents provided qualified support, with strain measures of the three specified types having a relatively substantial effect on delinquency and drug use, and the effect of those measures conditioned by association with delinquent peers and by self-efficacy as the theory predicted. The lesson reports these as the authors stated them, including the word 'qualified'. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Building on the Foundation of General Strain Theory: Specifying the Types of Strain Most Likely to Lead to Crime and Delinquency, Journal of Research in Crime and Delinquency 38(4):319-361 (November 2001)
sourceRecords.notes: Publisher abstract retrieved verbatim through the Crossref API on 2026-08-19; full text paywalled. Supports two things the lesson needs. First, the four characteristics that make a strain criminogenic: strains are most likely to result in crime when they are seen as unjust, are seen as high in magnitude, are associated with low social control, and create some pressure or incentive to engage in criminal coping. Second, the measurement problem stated by the theory's own author: researchers have little guidance when selecting among the many hundreds of types of strain and have trouble explaining why only some of them are related to crime, and the article predicts that some types of strain that have dominated strain research are not related to crime while some neglected types are. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Strain, Economic Status, and Crime, chapter 11 in Alex R. Piquero (ed.), The Handbook of Criminological Theory (Wiley, 2015)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert Agnew, in John Wiley & Sons
sourceRecords.notes: The theory's own author reviewing both classic and general strain theory. Read in full on 2026-08-19; the copy read was a PDF posted on a CUNY BMCC course site (openlab.bmcc.cuny.edu), whose page footer identifies it as Piquero, A. R. (2015), The Handbook of Criminological Theory, John Wiley & Sons, copyright 2015. Supports: that classic strain theory is the tradition of Merton (1938), Cohen (1955) and Cloward and Ohlin (1960) and turns on economic success or the broader goal of middle-class status; that poorer individuals are said to face more goal blockage and relative deprivation; that classic strain theorists held criminal coping more likely among those with weak commitment to legitimate norms, who blame others for their strain, who associate with criminal peers especially gang members, and who have the skills and opportunities for crime; that general strain theory widens strain to any disliked event or condition falling into three groups and distinguishes objective from subjective strains; that strains lead to negative emotions such as anger and frustration which create pressure for corrective action; that criminogenic strains are high in magnitude, touch core goals, values, needs, identities or activities, are seen as unjust, and are easily resolved through crime; the full list of conditioning factors - poor coping skills and resources, few conventional social supports, low social control, disposition to criminal coping including criminal associates, beliefs favourable to crime, and traits such as low constraint and negative emotionality, and situations where the costs of crime seem low and the benefits high; and that studies of economic status and crime have produced mixed results, most suggesting economic status is unrelated or weakly related to individual offending, which prompted challenges to strain theory's validity from Hirschi (1969) and Kornhauser (1978), with Agnew arguing the relationship is modest over much of its range but substantial for the very poor. Copyrighted; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Empirical Status of Strain Theory, Journal of Crime and Justice 15(2):1-30 (1992)
sourceRecords.provider: Velmer S. Burton Jr. and Francis T. Cullen, Taylor & Francis
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract retrieved through the OpenAlex API on 2026-08-19 after Crossref returned no abstract and the publisher site blocked retrieval; full text paywalled. Supports the lesson's honest statement of the classic-strain record: that Merton's macro-level theory of social structure and anomie evolved into an individual-level strain theory rooting crime in blocked access to desired success goals; that empirical tests have yielded mixed results with the level of support varying by the measure used to operationalise strain; that methodological limitations of existing studies further complicate assessment; and that the authors urged criminologists to broaden the research agenda to a wider range of strainful life circumstances. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: A New Test of Classic Strain Theory, Justice Quarterly 13(4):681-704 (December 1996)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert Agnew, Francis T. Cullen, Velmer S. Burton Jr., T. David Evans and R. Gregory Dunaway, Taylor & Francis
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract retrieved through the OpenAlex API on 2026-08-19; publisher site blocked direct retrieval and the full text is paywalled. Supports: that the central variable of classic strain theory is the individual's level of dissatisfaction or frustration with monetary status; that this variable had been ignored in virtually all tests of the theory, which most often measured strain indirectly as the disjunction between aspirations and expectations; that in a sample of adults in Cincinnati dissatisfaction was highest among objectively deprived individuals and those who wanted a lot of money, expected little, and felt relatively deprived; that dissatisfaction had a positive effect on income-generating crime and drug use, strongest among those with criminal friends and beliefs conducive to crime; and that the authors described this as qualified support for classic strain theory unlike the findings in much previous research. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Assessing Messner and Rosenfeld's Institutional Anomie Theory: A Partial Test, Criminology 33(3):411-429 (August 1995)
sourceRecords.provider: Mitchell B. Chamlin and John K. Cochran, American Society of Criminology / Wiley
sourceRecords.notes: Publisher abstract retrieved verbatim through the Crossref API on 2026-08-19; full text paywalled. Supports the statement of institutional anomie theory and its first partial test: that in Crime and the American Dream Messner and Rosenfeld contend that culturally and structurally produced pressures to secure monetary rewards, coupled with weak controls from non-economic social institutions, promote high levels of instrumental crime, and that the effects of economic conditions on profit-related crime depend on the strength of non-economic institutions; and that this cross-sectional test on U.S. state data found considerable but indirect support, with the effects of poverty on property crime depending on structural indicators of the capacity of non-economic institutions to ameliorate economic deprivation. The lesson reports the support as indirect, as the authors did. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record verified through the OpenAlex API on 2026-08-19: Steven F. Messner and Richard Rosenfeld, Social Forces, volume 75, issue 4, June 1997, pages 1393-1416. sourceRecords.title: Strain and Juvenile Delinquency: A Critical Review of Agnew's General Strain Theory (NCJ 231684), abstract of Journal of Loss and Trauma 12(4):383-418 (July 2007)
sourceRecords.provider: National Criminal Justice Reference Service Virtual Library, Office of Justice Programs, U.S. Department of Justice
sourceRecords.notes: Government bibliographic record, retrieved and read with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-19. Supports: the existence and scope of a critical review of the empirical evidence on general strain theory accumulated between 1992 and 2003 by Giacinto Froggio, published July 2007; the published abstract's characterisation of Agnew's theory as a social-psychological interpretation of juvenile delinquency with a solid conceptual basis that has drawn a significant number of important surveys; and the abstract's statement that no evaluation of the state of the theory had been made until then and that the review was a first critical evaluation of its empirical status. The lesson uses this for the point that the theory's empirical status was still being assessed a decade after publication, and for the social-psychological characterisation; it asserts no specific finding from the article itself, which was not read. The corresponding NCJRS record for Agnew (1992), NCJ 136257, was checked in the same session and now redirects to the OJP homepage, so it is not registered here.
